notes.h: Research design, causal inference and validity
notes.body:
A research design is the plan that links a question to evidence: which units are compared, what is observed, and how rival explanations are ruled out. Design matters more than technique. No estimator can rescue a comparison that cannot separate a cause from a confounder.

Key ideas
- Descriptive questions ask what is the case ("how polarised is the electorate?"). Causal questions ask what difference X makes to Y.
- Potential outcomes (the Neyman–Rubin framework): every unit has an outcome under treatment, Y(1), and one under control, Y(0). The individual causal effect is Y(1) − Y(0).
- The fundamental problem of causal inference (Holland 1986): only one potential outcome is ever observed for each unit. Causal effects must therefore be estimated by comparing groups that are alike in every respect except treatment.
- Threats to causal claims: confounding (a third variable drives both X and Y), reverse causation, selection bias and chance.
- Internal validity asks whether the effect is correctly identified within the study. External validity asks whether it generalises to other units, places and times.

Authorities
- King, Keohane and Verba, Designing Social Inquiry (1994): qualitative and quantitative research share one logic of inference. Researchers should increase the number of observable implications and avoid selecting on the dependent variable.
- Brady and Collier (eds), Rethinking Social Inquiry (2004): a reply defending distinctive qualitative tools such as causal-process observations.
- Mill, A System of Logic (1843): the methods of agreement and difference, the ancestors of most-different and most-similar designs.
- Robinson (1950): the ecological fallacy, which means inferring individual-level relationships from aggregate data.

Illustration
Democracies rarely fight one another. Is democracy the cause? Rival explanations include shared wealth, alliances and trade (confounders), and the possibility that a peaceful neighbourhood lets democracy take root (reverse causation). A credible design has to deal with each of these, for example by controlling for trade and alliance ties, or by checking whether peace came before or after democratisation.

Common pitfalls
- Treating a correlation as causal without naming the rival explanations and dealing with them.
- Confusing internal with external validity. A flawless lab experiment can still generalise poorly.
- Studying only cases where the outcome occurred, such as revolutions only. This removes the variation needed to test a cause.
- The ecological fallacy. Constituencies with more graduates voting Remain does not, on its own, show that graduates voted Remain.

From concept to indicator
Adcock and Collier (2001) describe measurement as a chain. It runs from a background concept (all the meanings of 'democracy'), to a systematised concept (an explicit definition), to indicators, and finally to scores for cases. Validity can fail at any link.

- Conceptualisation means defining the concept. Sartori (1970) warned against conceptual stretching, which is applying a concept to cases it does not fit. His ladder of abstraction shows a trade-off: concepts with fewer defining attributes cover more cases but say less about each.
- Operationalisation means choosing observable indicators.
- Reliability is consistency. The same procedure should give the same score when repeated or when used by different coders (inter-coder reliability, often reported with Cohen's kappa).
- Validity is whether the indicator captures the intended concept. Types include content, convergent/discriminant and construct validity.
- A measure can be reliable but invalid, like a scale that is always 2 kg out. A highly unreliable measure cannot be valid in any useful sense.

Levels of measurement (Stevens 1946)
- Nominal: categories with no order, such as party identification.
- Ordinal: ordered categories with unknown gaps, such as Likert agreement scales.
- Interval: equal gaps but an arbitrary zero, such as temperature in °C.
- Ratio: equal gaps and a true zero, such as turnout % or GDP per head.
The level of measurement decides which statistics make sense. The mean of party codes is meaningless.

Measurement error
- Random error in an explanatory variable biases regression slopes towards zero (attenuation bias). Random error in the outcome mainly widens standard errors.
- Systematic error pushes scores in one direction, for example respondents over-reporting that they voted.

Common datasets
- Polity (regime scores from −10 to +10; the latest Polity5 release runs only to 2018, so use V-Dem or Freedom House for recent years), Freedom House (political rights and civil liberties ratings), V-Dem (indices built from expert surveys, including the 0–1 electoral democracy 'polyarchy' index), Correlates of War (interstate conflict), ParlGov (parties and cabinets) and the Manifesto Project (party programmes).

Illustration
Defining democracy as 'holds elections' would count many electoral authoritarian regimes as democracies. That measure is over-inclusive and so invalid. Adding contestation and civil liberties improves validity, but it needs coder judgement, so reliability then has to be checked.

Common pitfalls
- Confusing reliability with validity.
- Treating ordinal scales as if the gaps were equal without saying why.
- Assuming democracy indices are interchangeable. They correlate highly overall but disagree at the margins, which is where many interesting cases sit.

Descriptive statistics summarise data before any inference is attempted. Exams test both the calculations and the judgement about which summary fits the data.

Central tendency
- Mean x̄ = Σx / n. Sensitive to outliers.
- Median: the middle value of the ordered data. Robust to outliers, so it is preferred for skewed variables such as income or donations.
- Mode: the most frequent value. It is the only meaningful average for nominal data.

Dispersion and shape
- Range, and the interquartile range (IQR = Q3 − Q1).
- Sample variance s² = Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1). Standard deviation s = √s².
- z-score z = (x − x̄) / s gives the number of standard deviations a value lies from the mean.
- Skew: right (positive) skew pulls the mean above the median.
- For a normal distribution, about 68% of values lie within 1 SD of the mean and 95% within 1.96 SD.

Two variables
- Cross-tabulations for categorical variables. Calculate percentages within each category of the explanatory variable, then compare across them.
- Covariance, and Pearson's r = cov(x, y) / (sₓ s_y). r runs from −1 to +1 and measures only linear association.
- Always plot first. Anscombe (1973) built four datasets with almost identical means, variances and correlations but completely different scatterplots.

Worked example
Turnout (%) in five wards: 30, 40, 45, 50, 85.
- Mean = 250 / 5 = 50. Median = 45.
- Deviations: −20, −10, −5, 0, 35. Squares: 400, 100, 25, 0, 1225. Sum = 1750.
- s² = 1750 / 4 = 437.5, so s ≈ 20.9.
- The ward at 85 has z = 35 / 20.9 ≈ 1.67.
The mean is above the median because of the high value, which is a sign of right skew. Dropping the outlier moves the mean to 41.25 but the median only to 42.5.

Common pitfalls
- Reporting means for nominal or ordinal codes.
- Reading r as a slope, or taking r ≈ 0 to mean no relationship. A strong curved relationship can give r near zero.
- Percentaging a cross-tab the wrong way, so that the outcome categories rather than the explanatory categories sum to 100.
- Dividing by n instead of n − 1 for a sample variance.
- Forgetting units. A standard deviation is in the same units as the data, while a variance is in squared units.

The linear model
Y = α + βX + ε. Ordinary least squares (OLS) chooses α̂ and β̂ to minimise the sum of squared residuals Σ(Y − Ŷ)². In the bivariate case β̂ = cov(X, Y) / var(X) and α̂ = Ȳ − β̂X̄.
- β̂ is the expected change in Y for a one-unit increase in X. In multiple regression this holds the other included variables constant.
- R² is the share of the variance in Y that the model accounts for. A low R² does not by itself make a slope estimate wrong.
- Inference: t = β̂ / SE. The p-value is the probability of an estimate at least this extreme if the true β were 0. In large samples a 95% confidence interval is roughly β̂ ± 1.96 SE.

Assumptions
- Gauss–Markov conditions: linear in parameters, random sampling, no perfect multicollinearity, zero conditional mean E(ε | X) = 0, and homoskedasticity. Under these, OLS is the best linear unbiased estimator.
- Zero conditional mean is what unbiasedness depends on. Heteroskedasticity leaves estimates unbiased but makes the usual standard errors wrong, so robust (or clustered) standard errors are used. Normal errors matter only for exact small-sample inference.

Omitted variable bias
If Z affects Y and is correlated with X but is left out, β̂ is biased. The sign of the bias is (sign of Z's effect on Y) × (sign of the correlation between X and Z).

Extensions
- Dummy variables: each coefficient is the difference from the reference category.
- Interactions: Y = α + β₁X + β₂Z + β₃XZ. The effect of X is β₁ + β₃Z, so β₁ alone is the effect of X only when Z = 0 (Brambor, Clark and Golder 2006).
- Logged variables, and logit or probit models for binary outcomes. Their raw coefficients are not marginal effects.
- Unit fixed effects in panel data remove confounders that do not change over time.

Worked example
Turnout% = 20 + 0.5 × (% graduates). The slope's SE is 0.1, so t = 5 and the slope is significant at 5%. A ward with 40% graduates is predicted to have 20 + 0.5 × 40 = 40% turnout. A 10-point rise in graduates goes with a predicted 5-point rise in turnout. This is an association, not proof of cause.

Common pitfalls
- Confusing statistical significance with substantive importance.
- Reading conditional coefficients in an interaction model as if they were overall effects.
- Controlling for post-treatment variables (mediators or colliders), which biases the estimate.
- Predicting far outside the observed range of X.
- Taking a high R² as evidence of causation.

Why randomise?
Random assignment makes treatment independent of potential outcomes. In expectation, the treatment and control groups are then alike on every characteristic, observed or not. The difference in group means is an unbiased estimate of the average treatment effect (ATE).

Types of experiment
- Laboratory experiments: high control, artificial setting.
- Field experiments: real settings. Gerber and Green (2000) randomly assigned New Haven voters to get-out-the-vote contact. Door-to-door canvassing raised turnout, direct mail had a small effect, and telephone calls had little or none.
- Survey experiments: randomised wording, vignettes, list experiments for sensitive questions, and conjoint designs (Hainmueller, Hopkins and Yamamoto 2014).

Complications
- Non-compliance. The intention-to-treat (ITT) effect is the effect of being assigned. With one-sided non-compliance, the complier average causal effect is CACE = ITT ÷ share of the treatment group actually treated.
- SUTVA (the stable unit treatment value assumption): one unit's treatment must not affect another's outcome. Spillovers within households break it.
- Attrition, Hawthorne effects, and ethical and practical limits on what can be randomised.

Quasi-experimental designs
- Natural experiments: nature, history or policy assigns treatment 'as if' at random (Dunning 2012).
- Difference-in-differences (DiD): (Ȳ treated after − Ȳ treated before) − (Ȳ control after − Ȳ control before). It relies on parallel trends: without treatment, both groups would have moved in the same way. Card and Krueger (1994) compared fast-food employment in New Jersey, which raised its minimum wage, with neighbouring Pennsylvania.
- Regression discontinuity (RD): treatment is set by a cutoff, so units just either side are compared. Lee (2008) used close US House races to estimate the incumbency advantage. It requires that units cannot sort precisely around the threshold.
- Instrumental variables (IV): the instrument must shift treatment (relevance) and affect the outcome only through treatment (the exclusion restriction). It identifies a local average treatment effect.

Worked example
A council brings in all-postal voting and turnout rises from 40% to 48%. In a comparison council it rises from 42% to 45%. DiD = (48 − 40) − (45 − 42) = 8 − 3 = 5 percentage points.

Common pitfalls
- Comparing those who complied with those who did not. This throws away the randomisation.
- Forgetting that an RD estimate applies only near the cutoff.
- Asserting parallel trends without checking the pre-treatment trends.
- Claiming the exclusion restriction can be tested directly. It has to be argued for.

Key terms
The population is who you want to learn about. The sampling frame is the list you can actually draw from. The sample is who is selected, and the respondents are who actually take part. Each gap between these is a possible source of bias.

Sampling designs
- Probability samples give every unit a known, non-zero chance of selection.
  - Simple random and systematic sampling.
  - Stratified: sample within subgroups (e.g. regions). Usually improves precision.
  - Cluster: sample groups (e.g. postcode sectors), then individuals within them. Cheaper but less precise; the loss is measured by the design effect.
  - Multistage designs combine these, as in face-to-face British Election Study surveys.
- Non-probability samples (quota, convenience, opt-in online panels) depend on modelling and weighting to represent the population.

Sampling error
For a proportion p from a simple random sample of size n, SE = √(p(1 − p) / n), and the 95% margin of error is about 1.96 × SE.
- Worked example: n = 1,000 and p = 0.5 give SE = √(0.25 / 1000) ≈ 0.0158, so the margin of error is about ±3.1 points. Quadrupling n to 4,000 halves it to about ±1.5 points.
- The margin of error on the lead between two parties is larger than the margin on either party's share.

Total survey error
- Coverage error: the frame misses part of the population.
- Nonresponse error: those who respond differ from those who do not.
- Measurement error: wording, question order, mode and interviewer effects; social desirability bias (such as over-reporting turnout); acquiescence bias.
- Processing and adjustment error.

Landmark failures
- Literary Digest, 1936: more than two million returned ballots wrongly predicted that Landon would beat Roosevelt. A skewed frame and self-selected response caused it. A bigger sample does not cure bias.
- UK general election, 2015: the polls underestimated the Conservative lead. The British Polling Council/Market Research Society inquiry (Sturgis et al. 2016) found unrepresentative samples were the main cause, rather than late swing or 'shy Tories'.

Design choices
- Cross-sections versus panels. Panels, such as the BES Internet Panel, re-interview the same people, so they can track individual change. They suffer from attrition and panel conditioning.
- Weighting matches the sample to known population totals. It reduces bias only if the weighting variables are related to both response and the outcome, and it increases variance.

Common pitfalls
- Treating the margin of error as if it covered all error.
- Believing a larger sample fixes a biased frame.
- Applying simple-random-sample formulas to cluster or opt-in samples without adjustment.
- Inferring individual change from repeated cross-sections.

What a case study is
Gerring (2004) defines a case study as an in-depth look at one unit, undertaken to shed light on a wider population of similar units. Its strengths are conceptual validity, tracing causal mechanisms, generating hypotheses and handling complex interactions. Its weaknesses are limited generalisability and the problem of many variables with few cases (Lijphart 1971).

Case selection
- Seawright and Gerring (2008) list techniques including typical, deviant, extreme, influential, most-similar and most-different cases.
- Crucial cases (Eckstein 1975) come in two kinds. A theory that fails in a most-likely case is badly damaged. A theory that survives a least-likely case is strongly supported.
- Comparative designs (Przeworski and Teune 1970) draw on Mill's methods. In a most similar systems design, cases share most features but differ in the outcome, so the explanation is sought among the few differences. A most different systems design looks for a common factor among otherwise dissimilar cases.
- Selection bias: Geddes (1990) showed how selecting cases on the dependent variable can produce false conclusions.

Process tracing
Process tracing examines the sequence of events within a case to test whether a proposed causal mechanism actually operated (George and Bennett 2005). Van Evera (1997) classified the tests, and Collier (2011) set them out as a framework:
- Straw-in-the-wind: neither necessary nor sufficient for confirming the hypothesis. Weak either way.
- Hoop: the hypothesis must pass it. Failing eliminates the hypothesis; passing does not confirm it.
- Smoking gun: passing strongly confirms the hypothesis; failing does not eliminate it.
- Doubly decisive: confirms the hypothesis and eliminates its rivals.

Other methods
- Elite and semi-structured interviews. These raise issues of access, sampling, self-serving accounts and the need to triangulate.
- Ethnography and participant observation, and archival research.
- Qualitative Comparative Analysis (Ragin 1987): a set-theoretic method that finds combinations of conditions sufficient for an outcome. It allows for conjunctural causation and equifinality, meaning several paths to the same outcome.

Illustration
Hypothesis: a government's spending cuts were driven by IMF loan conditions. A hoop test asks whether loan negotiations began before the cuts were decided. If not, the hypothesis fails. A smoking-gun test would be cabinet minutes recording that the cuts were adopted to meet the loan's terms.

Common pitfalls
- Claiming statistical generalisation from a single case.
- Selecting cases on the outcome.
- Confusing hoop tests with smoking-gun tests.
- Treating interview testimony as neutral evidence.

Core principles
- The Belmont Report (1979) sets out three principles. Respect for persons means informed consent and protecting those with reduced autonomy. Beneficence means minimising harm and maximising benefit. Justice means a fair distribution of research burdens and benefits.
- The ESRC Framework for Research Ethics, the UK social-science standard, has six principles. Research should maximise benefit and minimise harm. It should respect individuals' rights and dignity. Participation should be voluntary and properly informed. Research should be done with integrity and transparency. Lines of responsibility should be clear. Research should be independent, with any unavoidable conflicts of interest declared.
- The APSA Principles and Guidance for Human Subjects Research (2020) address political science directly, including research that affects political processes.

Law and governance in the UK
- University research ethics committees review projects before fieldwork begins.
- Under the UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018, political opinions are special category data. Processing them needs a lawful basis plus an extra condition, and research safeguards apply. Pseudonymised data still count as personal data; fully anonymised data do not.

Recurring issues
- Informed consent, and deception. Deception is generally acceptable only if it is necessary, carries little risk and is followed by a debrief.
- Confidentiality (the researcher knows who said what but does not disclose it) is different from anonymity (no one, including the researcher, can link data to a person).
- Vulnerable participants, conflict zones and authoritarian settings raise risks for participants and researchers, including digital security.
- Interventions in real politics. In 2014, researchers from Stanford and Dartmouth sent Montana voters mailers carrying the state seal before a non-partisan judicial election. They were criticised for misleading voters and possibly affecting the result.
- Online experiments: the Facebook 'emotional contagion' study (Kramer, Guillory and Hancock 2014) altered users' news feeds without specific consent.

Integrity and transparency
- LaCour and Green's 2014 Science article on canvassing and attitudes to same-sex marriage was retracted in 2015, after irregularities showed the survey data had not been collected as described.
- Responses to such cases include pre-registration and pre-analysis plans, sharing replication data and code (the 2014 DA-RT Journal Editors' Transparency Statement), and attention to p-hacking and publication bias.

Illustration
A student interviewing opposition activists in an authoritarian state should consider recording oral rather than signed consent, because a signed form creates a dangerous record. Other steps are encrypted storage, pseudonyms, and caution about details that could identify someone.

Common pitfalls
- Treating anonymity and confidentiality as the same thing.
- Assuming that ethics approval ends the researcher's responsibility.
- Ignoring harm to third parties or to the researcher.
- Assuming that public social media data raise no ethical questions.

cards.f: What is the fundamental problem of causal inference?
cards.b: For any unit we can observe only one potential outcome, either under treatment or under control, never both. Individual causal effects are therefore never directly observed (Holland 1986).

cards.f: Define the individual causal effect in the potential outcomes framework.
cards.b: Y(1) − Y(0): the difference between a unit's outcome if treated and the same unit's outcome if untreated.

cards.f: Internal vs external validity
cards.b: Internal validity asks whether the study correctly identifies the causal effect for the units studied. External validity asks whether that effect generalises to other populations, settings and times.

cards.f: What is a confounder?
cards.b: A variable that causes both the explanatory variable and the outcome. If it is not accounted for, it creates a spurious or distorted association between them.

cards.f: What is the ecological fallacy?
cards.b: Inferring individual-level relationships from aggregate-level data. Robinson (1950) showed that correlations across US states could differ sharply from the corresponding individual-level correlations.

cards.f: Why is selecting on the dependent variable a problem?
cards.b: If only cases where the outcome occurred are studied, there is no variation in the outcome. You cannot show that the supposed cause is more common where the outcome occurs than where it does not, and estimates are biased.

cards.f: What is the central claim of King, Keohane and Verba (1994)?
cards.b: Qualitative and quantitative research share a single logic of inference. Good design maximises observable implications, avoids selection bias and reports uncertainty.

cards.f: Mill's method of difference
cards.b: Compare cases that are alike in all relevant respects except one factor and the outcome. The factor that differs is the candidate cause. It is the basis of the most similar systems design.

cards.f: Give the two main non-causal explanations for an observed X–Y correlation, besides chance.
cards.b: Confounding (a third variable Z drives both X and Y) and reverse causation (Y actually drives X). Selection processes can also produce spurious associations.

cards.f: Why is the democratic peace a hard causal claim to establish?
cards.b: Democracy is not randomly assigned. Wealth, alliances and trade may cause both democracy and peace, and a peaceful environment may itself encourage democratisation, which is reverse causation.

cards.f: Reliability vs validity
cards.b: Reliability is consistency: repeated use or different coders give the same scores. Validity is whether the measure actually captures the intended concept. A measure can be reliable yet invalid.

cards.f: Name Stevens's four levels of measurement.
cards.b: Nominal (unordered categories), ordinal (ordered categories, unequal or unknown gaps), interval (equal gaps, arbitrary zero), and ratio (equal gaps, true zero).

cards.f: What is conceptual stretching (Sartori 1970)?
cards.b: Applying a concept to cases it does not really fit, so that it loses its meaning. Sartori's ladder of abstraction trades the number of defining attributes against the number of cases covered.

cards.f: Outline Adcock and Collier's (2001) measurement chain.
cards.b: Background concept → systematised concept → indicators → scores for cases. Measurement validity concerns whether the scores meaningfully capture the systematised concept.

cards.f: What does random measurement error in an explanatory variable do to an OLS slope?
cards.b: It biases the slope towards zero, which is called attenuation bias. Random error in the dependent variable mainly reduces precision rather than biasing the slope.

cards.f: What scale does Polity use?
cards.b: A 21-point scale from −10 (most autocratic) to +10 (most democratic), formed by subtracting the autocracy score from the democracy score. Note that the latest release (Polity5) covers only up to 2018.

cards.f: What is V-Dem and how is it built?
cards.b: Varieties of Democracy: a dataset that measures many dimensions of democracy using country-expert surveys, combined with a measurement model. It includes the 0–1 electoral democracy (polyarchy) index.

cards.f: Give an example of systematic measurement error in political surveys.
cards.b: Overreporting of turnout. Social desirability leads some non-voters to say they voted, so survey turnout is consistently above official turnout.

cards.f: Why should you not take the mean of party ID codes (1 = Lab, 2 = Con, 3 = LD)?
cards.b: Party ID is nominal. The numbers are arbitrary labels with no order or distance, so the mode or the category proportions are the right summaries.

cards.f: What is inter-coder reliability?
cards.b: The degree to which independent coders assign the same codes to the same material. It is often measured with Cohen's kappa, which corrects agreement for chance.

cards.f: Formula for the sample variance
cards.b: s² = Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1). Dividing by n − 1 corrects the downward bias that comes from using the sample mean.

cards.f: When is the median preferable to the mean?
cards.b: When the distribution is skewed or has outliers (e.g. income, campaign donations), because the median is not pulled towards extreme values.

cards.f: What is a z-score?
cards.b: z = (x − x̄) / s, the number of standard deviations a value lies above or below the mean.

cards.f: In a right-skewed distribution, how do the mean and median compare?
cards.b: The mean is usually greater than the median, because the long right tail pulls the mean upward.

cards.f: What does Pearson's r measure, and what are its limits?
cards.b: The strength and direction of a linear association, from −1 to +1. It misses non-linear relationships, is sensitive to outliers, and is not the slope.

cards.f: What is the lesson of Anscombe's quartet (1973)?
cards.b: Four datasets with almost identical means, variances, correlations and regression lines look completely different when plotted. Always visualise your data.

cards.f: How should you percentage a cross-tabulation?
cards.b: Calculate percentages within each category of the explanatory variable, then compare across those categories. For example, the share voting Leave within each age group.

cards.f: Approximately what share of a normal distribution lies within ±1 SD and ±1.96 SD?
cards.b: About 68% lies within ±1 SD and 95% within ±1.96 SD of the mean.

cards.f: Calculate the mean and median of 2, 4, 4, 5, 15.
cards.b: Mean = 30 / 5 = 6. Median = 4. The outlier 15 pulls the mean above the median.

cards.f: What is the interquartile range and why is it useful?
cards.b: IQR = Q3 − Q1, the spread of the middle 50% of the data. It is robust to outliers, unlike the range or standard deviation.

cards.f: What does OLS minimise?
cards.b: The sum of squared residuals, Σ(Yᵢ − Ŷᵢ)².

cards.f: Bivariate OLS slope formula
cards.b: β̂ = cov(X, Y) / var(X), and the intercept α̂ = Ȳ − β̂X̄.

cards.f: Interpret a coefficient of 0.3 on 'years of education' predicting a 0–10 left–right self-placement, controlling for age and income.
cards.b: Holding age and income constant, each extra year of education is associated with a 0.3-point higher predicted self-placement score. It is an association unless the design supports a causal reading.

cards.f: What is omitted variable bias, and when does it occur?
cards.b: Bias in a coefficient when a variable that affects Y and is correlated with X is left out of the model. Both conditions must hold.

cards.f: Which OLS assumption is key for unbiasedness?
cards.b: Zero conditional mean: E(ε | X) = 0. The error must be unrelated to the explanatory variables. Omitted confounders violate it.

cards.f: What does heteroskedasticity do to OLS?
cards.b: Coefficient estimates remain unbiased, but the conventional standard errors are wrong, so robust (heteroskedasticity-consistent) standard errors should be used.

cards.f: In Y = α + β₁X + β₂Z + β₃XZ, what is the marginal effect of X?
cards.b: ∂Y/∂X = β₁ + β₃Z. β₁ alone is the effect of X only when Z = 0 (Brambor, Clark and Golder 2006).

cards.f: What does R² tell you, and what doesn't it tell you?
cards.b: The proportion of variance in Y accounted for by the model. It says nothing about whether coefficients are unbiased or causal, and a low R² can coexist with a precisely estimated slope.

cards.f: Interpret a dummy variable coefficient of −4 for 'Scotland' (reference: England) in a turnout model.
cards.b: Holding other variables constant, predicted turnout in Scotland is 4 percentage points lower than in England, the reference category.

cards.f: Why not control for a post-treatment variable?
cards.b: Conditioning on a mediator removes part of the effect you want to estimate. Conditioning on a collider can create spurious associations. Either way the coefficient on the treatment is biased.

cards.f: What do unit fixed effects remove in panel regression?
cards.b: All time-invariant differences between units, observed or unobserved, such as a country's geography or colonial history. Identification then comes from within-unit change over time.

cards.f: Why does random assignment allow causal inference?
cards.b: It makes treatment independent of potential outcomes, so in expectation the groups are balanced on all observed and unobserved characteristics. The difference in means then estimates the ATE without bias.

cards.f: Intention-to-treat (ITT) vs complier average causal effect (CACE)
cards.b: ITT is the effect of being assigned to treatment, regardless of receipt. With one-sided non-compliance, CACE = ITT / share of the treatment group actually treated.

cards.f: What is SUTVA?
cards.b: The stable unit treatment value assumption: a unit's outcome depends only on its own treatment status (no interference or spillovers), and there is only one version of the treatment.

cards.f: Difference-in-differences formula
cards.b: DiD = (Ȳ_T,after − Ȳ_T,before) − (Ȳ_C,after − Ȳ_C,before). It identifies the effect under the parallel trends assumption.

cards.f: What is the parallel trends assumption?
cards.b: Without treatment, the treated and control groups would have followed the same trend in the outcome. It is untestable for the post-treatment period but can be probed with pre-treatment trends.

cards.f: What is a regression discontinuity design?
cards.b: Treatment is assigned by whether a running variable crosses a cutoff. Units just above and just below are compared, which gives a local effect at the threshold. Lee (2008) used close US House elections.

cards.f: Two conditions for a valid instrument
cards.b: Relevance: the instrument strongly affects treatment. Exclusion restriction: it affects the outcome only through treatment. Exclusion cannot be directly tested.

cards.f: What did Gerber and Green's (2000) New Haven study find?
cards.b: In a randomised field experiment, door-to-door canvassing substantially increased turnout, direct mail had a small effect, and telephone calls had little or no effect.

cards.f: What is a natural experiment?
cards.b: A study in which treatment is assigned by a process outside the researcher's control that is plausibly 'as if' random, such as lotteries or arbitrary borders (Dunning 2012).

cards.f: What is a list experiment used for?
cards.b: Measuring sensitive attitudes. The treatment group sees an extra sensitive item in a list and reports only how many items apply, so the difference in mean counts estimates prevalence without individual disclosure.

cards.f: Standard error of a sample proportion (SRS)
cards.b: SE = √(p(1 − p) / n). The 95% margin of error is about 1.96 × SE.

cards.f: Margin of error for p = 0.5, n = 1,000
cards.b: SE = √(0.25 / 1000) ≈ 0.0158, so the margin is about ±3.1 percentage points.

cards.f: Stratified vs cluster sampling
cards.b: Stratified: divide the population into groups and sample within every group, which usually improves precision. Cluster: randomly select whole groups and survey within them, which is cheaper but usually less precise.

cards.f: Why did the Literary Digest 1936 poll fail?
cards.b: Its frame (car and telephone owners, its own readers) and its self-selected responses over-represented Landon supporters. Over two million responses could not cure the biased frame and nonresponse.

cards.f: Main conclusion of the inquiry into the 2015 UK polling miss (Sturgis et al. 2016)
cards.b: The primary cause was unrepresentative samples, which held too many Labour voters and too few Conservatives. Late swing and other suspected factors made at most a modest contribution.

cards.f: Name the components of total survey error.
cards.b: Coverage error, sampling error, nonresponse error, measurement error (wording, mode, interviewer, social desirability), and processing or adjustment error.

cards.f: Panel vs repeated cross-section
cards.b: A panel re-interviews the same people, which allows individual-level change to be studied but suffers attrition and conditioning. Repeated cross-sections draw fresh samples, which shows aggregate change only.

cards.f: What does weighting do, and when does it help?
cards.b: It adjusts the sample to match known population margins. It reduces bias only if the weighting variables relate to both response and the outcome, and it increases variance.

cards.f: How does n affect the margin of error?
cards.b: The margin of error falls with √n, so quadrupling the sample size halves the margin of error.

cards.f: What is social desirability bias?
cards.b: Respondents giving answers they think are socially acceptable, for example overreporting voting or underreporting prejudice.

cards.f: Hoop test (process tracing)
cards.b: Evidence the hypothesis must pass. Failure eliminates it, but passing only keeps it alive and does not confirm it.

cards.f: Smoking-gun test
cards.b: Evidence that strongly confirms a hypothesis if found, but whose absence does not eliminate it.

cards.f: Doubly decisive test
cards.b: Evidence that both confirms the hypothesis and eliminates its rivals. It is rare in practice.

cards.f: Straw-in-the-wind test
cards.b: Evidence that is neither necessary nor sufficient. It slightly raises or lowers confidence in a hypothesis.

cards.f: Most similar systems design
cards.b: Compare cases that are alike on many background factors but differ on the outcome, then look for the explanatory factor that also differs. It applies Mill's method of difference.

cards.f: Most different systems design
cards.b: Compare cases that differ on many background factors but share the outcome, then look for the common factor. It applies Mill's method of agreement.

cards.f: What is a least-likely (crucial) case?
cards.b: A case where the theory's conditions are unfavourable. If the theory still holds there, confidence rises sharply (Eckstein 1975).

cards.f: What is process tracing?
cards.b: Within-case analysis of sequences and causal-process observations to test whether a hypothesised mechanism connects cause and outcome (George and Bennett 2005).

cards.f: What does Qualitative Comparative Analysis (QCA) do?
cards.b: It uses Boolean or fuzzy-set logic to find combinations of conditions that are necessary or sufficient for an outcome, allowing for equifinality and conjunctural causation (Ragin 1987).

cards.f: What is equifinality?
cards.b: Different combinations of causes can lead to the same outcome, so there is more than one causal path.

cards.f: Why use a deviant case?
cards.b: A case that does not fit an established theory or regression prediction can reveal omitted variables, new mechanisms or measurement problems.

cards.f: Three principles of the Belmont Report (1979)
cards.b: Respect for persons, beneficence and justice.

cards.f: Confidentiality vs anonymity
cards.b: Confidentiality: the researcher can identify participants but will not disclose their identities. Anonymity: no one, including the researcher, can link the data to an individual.

cards.f: When is deception in research generally considered acceptable?
cards.b: When it is necessary to answer the question, poses minimal risk, is approved by an ethics committee, and is followed by debriefing.

cards.f: Why are political opinions sensitive under UK data protection law?
cards.b: Under the UK GDPR they are special category data, so processing needs both a lawful basis and an additional condition (such as research with safeguards).

cards.f: What happened in the 2014 Montana election experiment?
cards.b: Stanford and Dartmouth researchers mailed voters information about a non-partisan judicial election bearing the state seal. Critics said it could mislead voters and affect the result.

cards.f: Why was LaCour and Green (2014) retracted?
cards.b: Irregularities showed that the survey data on canvassing and attitudes to same-sex marriage had not been collected as described. Science retracted the article in 2015.

cards.f: What is pre-registration?
cards.b: Publicly recording hypotheses, design and analysis plans before seeing outcome data, to limit p-hacking and selective reporting.

cards.f: What is p-hacking?
cards.b: Trying multiple specifications, samples or outcomes and reporting those that reach statistical significance, which inflates false-positive rates.

cards.f: Name three ESRC ethics principles.
cards.b: Maximise benefit and minimise harm; respect individuals' rights and dignity; make participation voluntary and properly informed. The others concern integrity and transparency, clear responsibility, and independence.

cards.f: Why might signed consent forms be inappropriate in an authoritarian setting?
cards.b: A signed form creates a written record linking the participant to the research, which could expose them to the state. Recorded oral consent may better protect participants.

questions.q: What is the 'fundamental problem of causal inference'?
options: Causal effects can only be estimated with experimental data
Only one potential outcome can be observed for each unit
Correlations between variables are always spurious
Samples are never perfectly representative of populations
questions.why: We see a unit's outcome either with the treatment or without it, never both, so individual effects can't be observed directly (Holland 1986). The other options either overstate the problem or describe something else.

questions.q: A survey item asks respondents to rate agreement from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree' on a five-point scale. At what level of measurement is this variable, strictly speaking?
questions.why: The categories have an order, but nothing guarantees the gaps between them are equal, so the scale is ordinal. Treating it as interval is a common simplification, but it has to be justified.

questions.q: For the values 10, 12, 14, 16, 48, which statement is correct?
questions.why: The sum is 100, so the mean is 100/5 = 20. The middle value is 14. The outlier 48 pulls the mean above the median.

questions.q: A researcher finds strong heteroskedasticity in an otherwise well-specified OLS model. What is the main consequence?
options: The conventional standard errors are unreliable
The model suffers from perfect multicollinearity
questions.why: Heteroskedasticity leaves OLS coefficients unbiased but makes the usual standard errors wrong. The standard fix is heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors.

questions.q: Turnout in a treated area rises from 40% to 50% after a reform, while in a comparison area it rises from 45% to 49%. What is the difference-in-differences estimate?
questions.why: DiD = (50 − 40) − (49 − 45) = 10 − 4 = 6 points. This counts as the effect only if the two areas would otherwise have followed parallel trends.

questions.q: A simple random sample of 2,500 voters finds 50% support for a policy. What is the approximate 95% margin of error?
In process tracing, which kind of test can eliminate a hypothesis if failed, but does little to confirm it if passed?
questions.why: A hoop test sets a necessary condition: the hypothesis must 'jump through the hoop' to stay alive. A smoking-gun test works the other way, confirming strongly if passed without eliminating if failed.

questions.q: A researcher knows which participant gave each interview but promises never to reveal identities in publications. This is best described as:
questions.why: Confidentiality means the researcher can identify participants but won't disclose who they are. Anonymity would mean nobody, the researcher included, could link responses to people.

questions.q: A researcher's measure of 'economic insecurity', used as an explanatory variable in OLS, contains substantial purely random measurement error. What is the most likely effect on its estimated coefficient?
options: No effect on the estimate or its precision
questions.why: Classical random error in a regressor causes attenuation bias, which shrinks the slope towards zero. Random error in the outcome variable would mainly inflate the variance.

questions.q: In a get-out-the-vote experiment, the treatment group's turnout is 4 points higher than the control group's, but only 40% of the treatment group were actually contacted (nobody in the control group was). What is the complier average causal effect (CACE)?
questions.why: CACE = ITT ÷ contact rate = 4 ÷ 0.4 = 10 points. This assumes one-sided non-compliance and that assignment affects turnout only through contact.

questions.q: In a regression of turnout (%) on a set of region dummies with London as the reference category, the coefficient on 'North East' is −5. What does this mean?
options: Turnout in the North East is 5%
Turnout in the North East is predicted to be 5 points lower than in London, holding other variables constant
Turnout in London is 5 points lower than in the North East
The North East explains 5% of the variance in turnout
questions.why: A dummy coefficient is the predicted difference from the omitted reference category, with the other regressors held constant.

questions.q: Distinguish internal validity from external validity, illustrating each with an example from political science.
markScheme: Defines internal validity: whether the causal effect is correctly identified for the units studied
Gives a relevant example of a threat to internal validity (e.g. confounding in observational data)
Defines external validity: whether the result generalises to other populations, settings or times
Gives a relevant example of an external validity concern (e.g. a lab experiment on students, or a single-city field experiment)
questions.modelAnswer: Internal validity asks whether a study has correctly identified the causal effect for the units it examined. An observational finding that canvassed voters turn out more may lack it if campaigns target people who were already likely to vote. External validity asks whether the result carries over to other populations, settings and times. Gerber and Green's New Haven experiment has strong internal validity because of randomisation, but its effect sizes may not transfer to a high-salience national election or to a country with different campaign norms.

questions.q: Explain the difference between reliability and validity in measurement, and explain why a measure can be reliable without being valid.
markScheme: Reliability defined as consistency across repetitions or coders
Validity defined as capturing the intended concept
Explains that consistent error (systematic bias) can produce reliable but invalid scores
Gives an appropriate political science example (e.g. 'holds elections' as a measure of democracy)
questions.modelAnswer: Reliability is consistency: repeated measurement, or measurement by different coders, gives the same scores. Validity is whether the scores capture the concept the researcher intends. A measure can be perfectly consistent and still systematically miss its target. Coding a country as democratic whenever it holds national elections is highly reliable, because coders will almost always agree. But it is invalid as a measure of democracy, because it classifies electoral authoritarian regimes with uncompetitive elections as democracies. Reliability is necessary for useful measurement but not sufficient.

questions.q: The number of written parliamentary questions tabled by five backbench MPs in a session is 8, 10, 12, 14 and 46. Calculate the mean, the median and the sample standard deviation, and state which measure of central tendency better represents a typical MP here, with a reason.
markScheme: Median = 12
Correct sum of squared deviations (100 + 64 + 36 + 16 + 784 = 1000)
Median preferred because the value 46 is an outlier that pulls the mean upwards
questions.modelAnswer: Mean = (8 + 10 + 12 + 14 + 46)/5 = 90/5 = 18. Median = 12. The deviations from the mean are −10, −8, −6, −4 and 28, and their squares are 100, 64, 36, 16 and 784, which sum to 1000. The sample variance is 1000/4 = 250, so s = √250 ≈ 15.8. The median better represents a typical MP. One unusually active MP (46 questions) pulls the mean above four of the five values, so the distribution is right-skewed and the mean is misleading.

questions.q: A researcher regresses MPs' rebellion rates on their majority size and finds a negative coefficient. She omits a variable measuring years since first election, which she believes increases rebellion and is positively correlated with majority size. Explain the likely direction of the resulting omitted variable bias.
markScheme: States both conditions for omitted variable bias (the omitted variable affects Y and is correlated with X)
Identifies that the effect of seniority on rebellion is positive
Identifies that the correlation between seniority and majority is positive
Concludes the bias is upward (positive), so the true effect of majority size is likely more negative than estimated
questions.modelAnswer: Omitted variable bias needs an omitted variable that both affects the outcome and is correlated with the included regressor. Both conditions hold here. Seniority increases rebellion (a positive effect on Y) and is positively correlated with majority size. The bias has the sign of the product of these two, so it is positive. Some of seniority's positive effect is wrongly credited to majority size, which pushes its coefficient upward. The estimated negative coefficient is therefore probably too close to zero, and the true effect of majority size is likely more negative.

questions.q: In a randomised canvassing experiment, 10,000 households are assigned to treatment and 10,000 to control. Turnout is 48% in the treatment group and 45% in the control group. Canvassers reached only 30% of treatment households, and no control household was contacted. Calculate the ITT and CACE, and explain why one should not simply compare contacted with uncontacted households.
markScheme: ITT = 48 − 45 = 3 percentage points
CACE = 3 ÷ 0.30 = 10 percentage points
States the assumptions (one-sided non-compliance; assignment affects turnout only via contact)
Explains that those contacted are self-selected (e.g. more often at home), so comparing them with the uncontacted reintroduces selection bias
questions.modelAnswer: The intention-to-treat effect is 48 − 45 = 3 percentage points. With one-sided non-compliance, the complier average causal effect is ITT divided by the contact rate: 3 ÷ 0.30 = 10 points. This assumes assignment affects turnout only through actual contact. Comparing contacted with uncontacted households would throw away the randomisation. Those who answer the door are not a random subset: they may be older, more settled or more politically engaged, all of which predict turnout. The difference would mix the canvassing effect with these pre-existing differences.

questions.q: Compare stratified sampling and cluster sampling, explaining the effect of each on the precision of survey estimates.
markScheme: Stratified: population divided into strata and a sample drawn within every stratum
Stratification usually increases precision, especially when strata differ on the outcome
Cluster: groups (e.g. postcode sectors) randomly selected, then units within them sampled
Clustering usually reduces precision (design effect > 1) because units within clusters are similar, but it lowers cost
questions.modelAnswer: In stratified sampling the population is divided into groups such as regions, and a random sample is drawn within every group. Each stratum is guaranteed to be represented, so precision usually improves, especially when strata differ on the variable of interest. In cluster sampling the researcher randomly selects whole groups, such as postcode sectors, and then samples within them. This cuts fieldwork costs for face-to-face surveys. But people in the same cluster tend to be similar, so each extra interview adds less new information. The design effect is above one and standard errors are larger than in a simple random sample of the same size.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a 'most-likely' and a 'least-likely' case, and the inferential value of each.
markScheme: Most-likely case: conditions strongly favour the theory's prediction
Failure in a most-likely case is strong disconfirming evidence
Least-likely case: conditions are unfavourable to the theory
Success in a least-likely case is strong confirming evidence (Eckstein's crucial case logic)
questions.modelAnswer: In a most-likely case the theory's conditions are all present and favourable, so the theory should clearly succeed. If it fails there, that is strong evidence against it. Success, by contrast, tells us little, since success was expected. In a least-likely case conditions are unfavourable. If the theory's prediction still holds, confidence in it rises sharply, because it has survived a hard test. Failure there is unsurprising and weakly informative. Both are forms of Eckstein's (1975) crucial-case reasoning, which lets a single case carry real weight in testing a theory.

questions.q: Identify three elements that should be included for consent to research participation to count as properly informed.
markScheme: Information about the purpose, procedures and what participation involves
Information about risks, and about how data will be stored, used and kept confidential
Statement that participation is voluntary and the participant may withdraw (within stated limits) without penalty
questions.modelAnswer: Participants must understand what the research is for and what they will be asked to do, including the time involved and whether sessions are recorded. They must be told about foreseeable risks and how their data will be handled: storage, who has access, anonymisation or pseudonymisation, and how results will be published. Finally, they must know that participation is voluntary and that they can withdraw without penalty, along with any practical limit, such as data already aggregated into analysis.

questions.q: What does a Pearson correlation coefficient of r = −0.8 between two variables tell you, and what does it not tell you?
markScheme: A strong negative linear association: as one variable rises, the other tends to fall
Does not show causation, the size of the slope, or the presence or absence of non-linear relationships
questions.modelAnswer: An r of −0.8 indicates a strong negative linear association: higher values of one variable tend to go with lower values of the other. It does not show that one causes the other. It does not give the slope, meaning how much Y changes per unit of X. And it measures only linear association, so it says nothing about non-linear patterns or whether outliers are driving the result.

questions.q: A polling company uses an opt-in online panel and weights its sample to match the population on age, sex and region. Explain why this may still fail to produce accurate vote-intention estimates, and suggest two improvements.
markScheme: Weighting only corrects bias if weighting variables are related to both participation and vote choice
Opt-in panellists may differ on unweighted traits (e.g. political interest), so bias remains within weighting cells
Weighting increases variance / reduces effective sample size
Improvement: weight on politically relevant variables (e.g. past vote, education, political attention)
Improvement: use probability-based recruitment, or model-based approaches such as MRP, and validate against benchmarks
questions.modelAnswer: Weighting removes bias only to the extent that the weighting variables explain both who joins the panel and how people vote. Within each age–sex–region cell, opt-in panellists tend to be more politically engaged than non-panellists. If engagement relates to vote choice, the bias survives weighting. This was a key lesson of the 2015 UK polling miss. Heavy weights also increase variance and shrink the effective sample size. Improvements include weighting on politically relevant variables such as past vote, education and political attention. Pollsters can also recruit by probability methods, or use multilevel regression and post-stratification, checked against known benchmarks.

questions.q: A think-tank reports that, across 200 constituencies, those where residents spend more time on social media saw larger increases in affective polarisation between 2017 and 2024 (r = 0.45). Its director, Martin Hale, concludes that 'social media is driving Britons apart' and calls for algorithmic regulation. Evaluate the research design behind this claim, and propose a design that would support a stronger causal inference.
markScheme: Identifies the claim as causal, while the evidence is an aggregate correlation
Ecological fallacy: constituency-level data cannot show that individual social media users polarised
Confounding: e.g. age, education, urbanity or local political competition may drive both
Reverse causation: already-polarised people may seek out political content online
Measurement issues: self-reported time online; how affective polarisation is measured
Notes r = 0.45 says nothing about effect size or mechanism; possible selection of time period
Proposes an individual-level panel with fixed effects to exploit within-person change
Proposes an experiment (e.g. randomised deactivation, as in some recent field studies) or a natural experiment (e.g. staggered broadband rollout)
Discusses the trade-off between internal and external validity of the proposed design
Reaches a justified overall judgement
questions.modelAnswer:
Hale makes a causal claim from a cross-sectional, aggregate correlation, and the design cannot support it.

First, the ecological fallacy. Data at constituency level cannot show that the individuals who use social media are the ones who polarised. Polarisation could be rising among non-users in high-use areas.

Second, confounding. Constituencies with heavy social media use are likely to be younger, more urban and more graduate-heavy, and these traits may independently affect how polarisation changed after 2017. Local factors such as close contests or Brexit salience could also drive both variables.

Third, reverse causation. People who are already polarised may spend more time consuming political content online. Measurement also matters. Self-reported screen time is noisy, and affective polarisation indices, such as feeling thermometers towards rival party supporters, depend on question format. An r of 0.45 describes the strength of linear association, not the size of any effect.

A stronger design would work at the individual level and break the link between selection and treatment. One option is a panel survey measuring each respondent's platform use and partisan affect repeatedly. With individual fixed effects, this removes stable traits such as personality and estimates how changes in use relate to changes in affect. Its weakness is that time-varying confounders remain. Better still is randomisation. Participants could be paid to deactivate a platform for several weeks, with polarisation compared against a control group. This gives high internal validity, but only for a short, partial reduction in use among volunteers. A natural experiment, such as the staggered rollout of broadband across areas, could add evidence about longer-term exposure.

On balance, the think-tank's evidence is suggestive but not causal. Policy should wait for designs that address selection, confounding and the level of analysis.

questions.q: 'Because the major democracy indices are highly correlated with one another, a researcher's choice between Polity, Freedom House and V-Dem makes little difference to their conclusions.' Discuss.
markScheme: Explains that high overall correlation is driven by clear-cut cases (stable democracies and closed autocracies)
Notes that the indices diverge most for hybrid / electoral authoritarian regimes, where much research interest lies
Discusses conceptualisation differences: Polity's focus on executive recruitment and constraints vs Freedom House's rights and liberties vs V-Dem's multiple conceptions
Discusses aggregation choices (additive scales, thresholds, Bayesian measurement models) and their consequences
Discusses measurement method: coders/expert surveys, reliability and possible bias
Uses Adcock and Collier's measurement chain or the validity/reliability distinction
Notes that continuous vs dichotomous measures (e.g. thresholds on Polity) affect findings
Recognises that robustness checks across indices are good practice
Considers that the choice should follow from the theoretical concept being tested
Reaches a reasoned judgement on the proposition
questions.modelAnswer:
The proposition holds for clear cases but fails where it matters most.

The major indices do correlate highly across all country-years, because most observations are clear-cut. Norway scores near the top on every index and North Korea near the bottom. Overall correlations, however, hide disagreement in the middle. Electoral authoritarian and hybrid regimes are where democracy indices most often diverge, and they are central to research on democratic backsliding, regime transitions and the democratic peace. If a study's leverage comes from these cases, the choice of index can change the results.

The divergence starts with conceptualisation. In Adcock and Collier's terms, the indices systematise different concepts. Polity focuses on institutional features: competitiveness of executive recruitment, constraints on the executive, and political participation. It says relatively little about civil liberties. Freedom House rates political rights and civil liberties, a thicker liberal conception. V-Dem separates several conceptions, including electoral, liberal, participatory, deliberative and egalitarian. It forces researchers to choose which concept their theory concerns.

Aggregation and method matter too. Polity combines component scores into a −10 to +10 scale. V-Dem pools many expert ratings through a measurement model and reports uncertainty around scores. Freedom House relies on analysts' ratings against a checklist. These choices affect reliability and can introduce systematic differences, for example when coders read institutional rules differently from practice.

The measure's form also matters. Collapsing a continuous scale into a democracy/autocracy dichotomy using a threshold, such as Polity at 6 or above, can reclassify borderline cases and change estimated effects.

The choice therefore often does make a difference. Good practice is to let theory determine the concept, choose the index whose systematised concept matches it, and report whether results hold across alternative measures. Robustness across indices strengthens a finding. Sensitivity to the index is itself informative, because it shows the result depends on how democracy is defined.

questions.q:
Researcher Amira Khan counts the number of active local campaign volunteers for the Green Party in five wards in each of two councils.
Northfield: 4, 6, 7, 8, 10
Southmere: 2, 3, 3, 4, 18
She writes: 'Mean volunteer numbers are similar in both councils, so the party's local organisation is about equally strong.' (a) Calculate the mean, median and sample standard deviation for each council. (b) Calculate the z-score of the Southmere ward with 18 volunteers. (c) Evaluate Khan's conclusion.
markScheme: Northfield mean = 35/5 = 7; median = 7
Northfield sum of squared deviations = 20; s² = 5; s ≈ 2.24
Southmere mean = 30/5 = 6; median = 3
Southmere sum of squared deviations = 182; s² = 45.5; s ≈ 6.75
Notes Southmere is right-skewed: mean well above median
Argues the medians show a typical Southmere ward has far fewer volunteers than a typical Northfield ward
Notes Southmere's organisation is concentrated in one ward (high dispersion), unlike Northfield's even spread
Raises small-n and measurement caveats (definition of 'active', counting method)
Concludes that Khan's claim is not supported
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Northfield: the sum is 35, so the mean is 7. The ordered values 4, 6, 7, 8, 10 give a median of 7. The deviations are −3, −1, 0, 1 and 3, with squares 9, 1, 0, 1 and 9, summing to 20. So s² = 20/4 = 5 and s = √5 ≈ 2.24.

Southmere: the sum is 30, so the mean is 6. The ordered values 2, 3, 3, 4, 18 give a median of 3. The deviations are −4, −3, −3, −2 and 12, with squares 16, 9, 9, 4 and 144, summing to 182. So s² = 182/4 = 45.5 and s ≈ 6.75.

(b) z = (18 − 6)/6.75 ≈ 1.78. The ward lies almost 1.8 standard deviations above Southmere's mean. In a sample this small, one extreme value also inflates the standard deviation itself, which keeps its z-score down.

(c) Khan's conclusion depends entirely on the mean, which is the wrong summary for Southmere. Its distribution is strongly right-skewed. A single ward with 18 volunteers lifts the mean to 6, but four of the five wards have between 2 and 4. The medians give a different picture: a typical Northfield ward has 7 volunteers and a typical Southmere ward has 3. Without the outlier, Southmere's mean would be 3.

The standard deviations also show that Northfield's organisation is spread evenly, while Southmere's is concentrated in one ward, perhaps a target seat or the home ward of a councillor. For campaigning across a whole council, that concentration is a real weakness. Five wards is also a tiny sample, and 'active volunteer' needs a clear and consistent definition across the two councils.

The data therefore suggest Northfield has the stronger and more even organisation. Khan should report medians and measures of spread, and look at the distributions, rather than compare means alone.

questions.q:
Dr Okafor regresses local election turnout (%) in 400 English local authority areas on three variables: the percentage of residents aged 65+, median household income (£000s), and a dummy for metropolitan areas. The results (standard errors in brackets) are: constant 32.0 (4.0); % aged 65+ 0.60 (0.15); income 0.25 (0.20); metropolitan −3.0 (1.0). R² = 0.35.
(a) Interpret each coefficient and assess its statistical significance. (b) Calculate a 95% confidence interval for the age coefficient. (c) Predict turnout for a non-metropolitan area with 20% aged 65+ and median income of £30,000, and for an otherwise identical metropolitan area. (d) Okafor concludes that 'older people are more likely to vote'. Evaluate this inference.
markScheme: Age: each extra percentage point of residents aged 65+ is associated with 0.6 points higher turnout, holding others constant; t = 4, significant at 5%
Income: £1,000 higher median income associated with 0.25 points higher turnout; t = 1.25, not significant at 5%
Metro: metropolitan areas predicted 3 points lower turnout; t = −3, significant
Constant interpreted with caution (all regressors = 0 is outside the data)
Non-metro prediction: 32 + 12 + 7.5 = 51.5%
Metro prediction: 48.5%
Ecological fallacy: area-level association does not establish that older individuals vote more
Omitted variables (e.g. home ownership, residential stability) may confound; R² = 0.35 is not itself the problem
Notes non-significance of income is not proof of no effect
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Holding income and metropolitan status constant, each additional percentage point of residents aged 65+ is associated with turnout 0.60 points higher. Its t-statistic is 0.60/0.15 = 4, so it is significant at the 5% level. A £1,000 rise in median income goes with 0.25 points higher turnout, but t = 0.25/0.20 = 1.25 is below 1.96. The estimate is not significant, which means the data cannot rule out a zero effect. It does not prove there is no effect. Metropolitan areas have predicted turnout 3 points lower than non-metropolitan areas with the same age profile and income (t = −3, significant). The constant of 32 is the prediction when all regressors are zero, an area with no older residents and no income, so it has no substantive meaning.

(b) 0.60 ± 1.96 × 0.15 = 0.60 ± 0.294, giving a 95% confidence interval of about 0.31 to 0.89.

(c) Non-metropolitan: 32 + 0.60 × 20 + 0.25 × 30 = 32 + 12 + 7.5 = 51.5%. Metropolitan: 51.5 − 3 = 48.5%.

(d) The conclusion makes an individual-level claim from area-level data, which is the ecological fallacy. Areas with many older residents might have high turnout because younger residents in those places also vote more, perhaps because the communities are stable and long-established. The age coefficient is also exposed to omitted variable bias. Home ownership and length of residence are correlated with an older population and plausibly raise turnout. If they are excluded, they would inflate the age coefficient. The modest R² is not itself evidence of bias, but it does show that much variation remains unexplained.

To test whether older people are more likely to vote, Okafor needs individual-level data, ideally validated turnout from survey respondents or marked electoral registers. Individual-level research does generally find higher turnout among older voters, but this aggregate regression cannot establish it.

questions.q:
Using cross-national survey data, Dr Lindqvist estimates support for redistribution (0–100) as a function of whether a respondent is economically insecure (a 0/1 dummy), the generosity of their country's welfare state (an index observed between 10 and 40), and their interaction:
Support = 50 + 8·Insecure − 0.2·Generosity − 0.25·(Insecure × Generosity).
A research assistant summarises: 'Insecurity raises support for redistribution by 8 points, and generous welfare states reduce support by 0.2 points per unit.' Critically assess this summary. Calculate the marginal effect of insecurity at generosity values of 10, 20, 32 and 40, interpret the pattern, and explain what further information would be needed for valid inference.
markScheme: Marginal effect of Insecure = 8 − 0.25 × Generosity
Correct values: 5.5 at G = 10; 3.0 at G = 20; 0 at G = 32; −2.0 at G = 40
8 is the effect only at G = 0, which is outside the observed range: an extrapolation
−0.2 is the effect of generosity only for secure respondents (Insecure = 0)
For insecure respondents the generosity effect is −0.2 − 0.25 = −0.45 per unit
Interprets the pattern: the insecurity gap shrinks as welfare generosity rises and may reverse
Notes that marginal-effect standard errors require the covariance of β₁ and β₃, not just individual SEs (Brambor, Clark and Golder 2006)
Recommends plotting marginal effects with confidence intervals across the observed range
Notes the constitutive terms should remain in the model and are not 'main effects'
Raises causal and design issues: country-level moderator with few countries, clustering of errors, endogeneity of generosity
Considers that the negative effect at G = 40 may be imprecise or reflect extrapolation near the edge of the data
Overall evaluation that the summary misreads conditional coefficients
questions.modelAnswer:
The summary misreads the interaction model. In Y = α + β₁Insecure + β₂Generosity + β₃(Insecure × Generosity), each constitutive coefficient is conditional, not an overall or 'main' effect.

The effect of insecurity is ∂Support/∂Insecure = 8 − 0.25 × Generosity.
- G = 10: 8 − 2.5 = 5.5 points
- G = 20: 8 − 5 = 3.0 points
- G = 32: 8 − 8 = 0 points
- G = 40: 8 − 10 = −2.0 points

The 8-point figure is the effect when generosity equals zero. That value lies outside the observed range of 10 to 40, so it describes no real country. Similarly, −0.2 is the effect of generosity only for secure respondents. For insecure respondents the generosity slope is −0.2 − 0.25 = −0.45 per unit.

Substantively, the gap in support between insecure and secure citizens is largest in lean welfare states and shrinks as generosity rises, disappearing at about 32. One reading is that generous welfare states already protect insecure people, which weakens their demand for more redistribution relative to secure citizens. The point estimate of −2 at G = 40 suggests a reversal, but it lies at the edge of the data and may be imprecise.

Valid inference needs more information. As Brambor, Clark and Golder (2006) stress, the standard error of a marginal effect is √(var(β̂₁) + G²var(β̂₃) + 2G·cov(β̂₁, β̂₃)), so the coefficient covariance is required. Marginal effects should be plotted with confidence intervals across the observed range of generosity, along with the distribution of the data. Generosity varies only between countries, so standard errors should be clustered by country. If there are few countries, the effective sample size for the moderator is small and a multilevel model may be appropriate. Finally, generosity is not randomly assigned. Countries with generous welfare states differ in culture, history and party systems, so the interaction describes conditional associations, not necessarily the causal moderating effect of welfare policy.

questions.q:
In 2022 the fictional region of Westmark introduced automatic voter registration (AVR). The neighbouring region of Eastvale did not. Turnout in regional elections, measured as a percentage of the voting-age population, was:
Westmark: 2014 30%, 2018 34%, 2022 45%
Eastvale: 2014 33%, 2018 37%, 2022 40%
The Westmark government claims AVR increased turnout by 11 points. (a) Calculate the naive before-after estimate, the post-reform cross-sectional difference, and the difference-in-differences estimate using 2018 and 2022. (b) Assess the parallel trends assumption using the data. (c) Evaluate the remaining threats to inference.
markScheme: Before-after: 45 − 34 = 11 points
Cross-sectional 2022 difference: 45 − 40 = 5 points
Explains why the before-after figure overstates the effect (a common trend of +3 in the comparison region)
Pre-trends 2014–18: both +4, so consistent with parallel trends
Notes that parallel pre-trends support but do not prove the counterfactual assumption
Notes the value of measuring turnout over voting-age population rather than registered voters (AVR inflates the register)
Threat: concurrent shocks specific to Westmark in 2022 (e.g. a competitive contest, other reforms)
Threat: one treated and one control unit, so statistical inference and generalisation are weak
Threat: spillovers or migration between regions; anticipation effects
Suggests improvements: more units, event-study, synthetic control, placebo tests
Reaches an overall judgement on the 11-point claim
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The naive before-after estimate is 45 − 34 = 11 points, the government's figure. The 2022 cross-sectional difference is 45 − 40 = 5 points, but Westmark always had lower turnout, so this comparison is biased downward. The difference-in-differences estimate is (45 − 34) − (40 − 37) = 11 − 3 = 8 points.

The before-after figure attributes all of Westmark's rise to AVR. Eastvale, without the reform, rose by 3 points over the same period. That suggests a general upward trend, perhaps from a more salient election, which DiD subtracts.

(b) Between 2014 and 2018, before the reform, both regions rose by exactly 4 points. This is consistent with parallel trends and makes Eastvale a plausible counterfactual. But two pre-periods is very little evidence. The assumption concerns the unobservable post-2018 path, and parallel past trends do not guarantee parallel future trends. Using voting-age population as the denominator is sensible. AVR mechanically enlarges the register, so turnout as a share of registered electors could fall even if more people voted.

(c) Several threats remain. A Westmark-specific shock in 2022, such as an unusually competitive contest, a high-profile candidate or another reform like expanded postal voting, would be wrongly credited to AVR. With one treated and one control region, the estimate cannot separate the reform from anything else unique to Westmark. Conventional standard errors would also be misleading. Population movement between regions or media spillovers could affect Eastvale. If politicians anticipated the reform, campaigning may have changed before 2022.

The design could be improved by adding more comparison regions, perhaps through a synthetic control built from several untreated regions. Other options are placebo tests on pre-reform years, and individual-level evidence on whether the newly registered actually voted.

Overall, the 11-point claim is overstated. Eight points is a more defensible estimate, but it should be treated as provisional given how thin the comparison is.

questions.q: 'Natural experiments and quasi-experimental designs have solved political science's problem of causal inference.' Discuss.
markScheme: Explains the fundamental problem of causal inference and the selection problem that these designs address
Explains natural experiments and the 'as if random' assumption (Dunning 2012)
Explains regression discontinuity with an example (e.g. Lee 2008 close elections) and its identifying assumption
Explains difference-in-differences and parallel trends; instrumental variables and the exclusion restriction
Credits these designs with substantially improving internal validity over conventional observational regression
Limits: local estimands (LATE, effect at the cutoff) and weak external validity
Limits: untestable assumptions (exclusion, parallel trends, no sorting) still require argument
Limits: the 'streetlight' problem: questions chosen for identification rather than importance; big structural questions (war, regime change) rarely have clean natural experiments
Limits: mechanisms remain unclear without qualitative or process evidence
Notes problems in practice: weak instruments, manipulation at thresholds, compound treatments
Considers complementary roles of theory, qualitative work and multi-method designs
Reaches a balanced, well-justified conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Quasi-experimental methods have greatly improved causal inference in political science, but 'solved' overstates what they achieve.

The core difficulty is that we never observe both potential outcomes for a unit, and in observational data treatment is usually chosen by people whose characteristics also affect outcomes. Natural experiments respond by finding situations where assignment is plausibly 'as if' random (Dunning 2012). Regression discontinuity compares units just either side of a cutoff. Lee (2008) used close US House races, in which narrowly winning or losing is close to a coin toss, to estimate the incumbency advantage. Difference-in-differences uses an untreated comparison group, and instrumental variables use a source of variation in treatment that affects outcomes only through treatment. Each replaces the implausible 'no unobserved confounders' assumption of conventional regression with a more targeted, and often more defensible, assumption.

Those assumptions remain assumptions. Parallel trends concerns an unobserved counterfactual. The exclusion restriction cannot be tested directly, and many instruments used in political science, such as rainfall or geography, plausibly affect outcomes through several channels. RD requires that units cannot precisely manipulate the running variable. Weak instruments and compound treatments add practical problems.

These designs also identify local quantities. An RD estimate applies to bare winners and losers. IV recovers effects for compliers. A natural experiment in one Indian state or one US city may not travel. There is a deeper worry about the agenda. Researchers may gravitate towards questions with a convenient identification strategy rather than important ones. Many central questions, such as why democracies collapse, the causes of war, or the effects of electoral systems, rarely come with clean exogenous variation.

Finally, credible identification of an effect does not reveal its mechanism. Process tracing, theory and qualitative fieldwork remain essential for understanding why effects occur and whether they generalise. Natural experiments are best seen as a powerful addition to a multi-method toolkit, not as a solution that replaces judgement.

questions.q:
A newspaper commissions a poll of 1,600 adults from an opt-in online panel, weighted to national targets. It reports Party X on 36% and Party Y on 32% under the headline 'Party X opens up clear lead'.
(a) Treating the data as a simple random sample, calculate the 95% margin of error for each party's share and for the lead. [Hint: for the difference between two shares from the same sample, var = (p₁ + p₂ − (p₁ − p₂)²) / n.] (b) The pollster estimates a design effect of 1.5 from weighting. Recalculate the margin of error on the lead. (c) Evaluate the headline and the sources of error that the margin of error does not capture.
markScheme: Notes the 4-point lead is roughly equal to its margin of error (z ≈ 1.94)
Design effect: effective n ≈ 1,067; SE of lead ≈ 0.0252; MoE ≈ ±4.9 points
Concludes 'clear lead' is not supported by the data
Explains that margins of error assume probability sampling; for opt-in panels they are at best a modelled approximation
Coverage and self-selection bias in opt-in panels
Nonresponse and weighting assumptions; 2015 polling miss (Sturgis et al. 2016)
Measurement error: turnout likelihood, question wording, 'don't knows'
Recommends looking at trends across polls and pollsters rather than a single poll
Overall evaluation
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Party X: SE = √(0.36 × 0.64 / 1600) = √0.000144 = 0.012, so MoE = 1.96 × 0.012 ≈ ±2.4 points.
Party Y: SE = √(0.32 × 0.68 / 1600) = √0.000136 ≈ 0.0117, so MoE ≈ ±2.3 points.
